{{Short description|Symmetry in statistical physics}}
The '''Kramers–Wannier duality''' is a [[symmetry]] in [[statistical physics]].  It relates the [[Thermodynamic free energy|free energy]] of a two-dimensional [[square-lattice Ising model]] at a low temperature to that of another Ising model at a high temperature.  It was discovered by [[Hendrik Anthony Kramers|Hendrik Kramers]] and [[Gregory Wannier]] in 1941.<ref>
*{{cite journal | doi=10.1103/PhysRev.60.252 | title=Statistics of the Two-Dimensional Ferromagnet. Part I | date=1941 | last1=Kramers | first1=H. A. | last2=Wannier | first2=G. H. | journal=Physical Review | volume=60 | issue=3 | pages=252–262 | bibcode=1941PhRv...60..252K }}
*{{cite journal | doi=10.1103/PhysRev.60.263 | title=Statistics of the Two-Dimensional Ferromagnet. Part II | date=1941 | last1=Kramers | first1=H. A. | last2=Wannier | first2=G. H. | journal=Physical Review | volume=60 | issue=3 | pages=263–276 | bibcode=1941PhRv...60..263K }}</ref>  With the aid of this duality Kramers and Wannier found the exact location of the [[critical point (thermodynamics)|critical point]] for the Ising model on the [[square lattice]].

Similar dualities establish relations between free energies of other statistical models.  For instance, in 3 dimensions the Ising model is dual to an Ising gauge model.

==Intuitive idea==

The 2-dimensional Ising model exists on a lattice, which is a collection of squares in a chessboard pattern.  With the finite lattice, the edges can be connected to form a torus.  In theories of this kind, one constructs an [[Involution (mathematics)|involutive transform]].  For instance, [[Lars Onsager]] suggested that the [[Star-Triangle transformation]] could be used for the triangular lattice.<ref>{{cite arXiv | eprint=cond-mat/9511003 | last1=Bhattacharjee | first1=Somendra M. | last2=Khare | first2=Avinash | title=Fifty Years of the Exact Solution of the Two-Dimensional Ising Model by Onsager | date=1995 }}</ref>  Now the dual of the ''discrete'' torus is [[dual lattice|itself]].  Moreover, the dual of a highly disordered system (high temperature) is a well-ordered system (low temperature).  This is because the [[Fourier transform]] takes a high [[Bandwidth (signal processing)|bandwidth]] signal (high [[standard deviation]]) to a low one (low standard deviation).  So one has essentially the same theory with an inverse temperature.  

When one raises the temperature in one theory, one lowers the temperature in the other.  If there is only one [[phase transition]], it will be at the point at which they cross, at which the temperatures are equal.  Because the 2D Ising model goes from a disordered state to an ordered state, there is a near [[one-to-one mapping]] between the disordered and ordered phases.

The theory has been generalized, and is now blended with many other ideas.  For instance, the square lattice is replaced by a circle,<ref>{{cite arXiv | eprint=cond-mat/9805301 | last1=Wu | first1=F. Y. | title=Self-dual property of the Potts model in one dimension | date=1998 }}</ref> random lattice,<ref>{{cite journal | arxiv=hep-lat/0110063 | last1=Bogacz | first1=L. | last2=Burda | first2=Z. | last3=Jurkiewicz | first3=J. | last4=Krzywicki | first4=A. | last5=Petersen | first5=C. | last6=Petersson | first6=B. | title=Dirac operator and Ising model on a compact 2D random lattice | journal=Acta Physica Polonica B | date=2001 | volume=32 | issue=12 | page=4121 | bibcode=2001AcPPB..32.4121B }}</ref> nonhomogeneous torus,<ref>{{cite arXiv | eprint=hep-th/9703037 | last1=Bugrij | first1=Anatolij I. | last2=Shadura | first2=Vitalij N. | title=Duality of the 2D Nonhomogeneous Ising Model on the Torus | date=1997 }}</ref> triangular lattice,<ref>{{cite journal | arxiv=cond-mat/0402420 | doi=10.1088/0305-4470/37/18/003 | title=Self-duality for coupled Potts models on the triangular lattice | date=2004 | last1=Richard | first1=Jean-François | last2=Jacobsen | first2=Jesper Lykke | last3=Picco | first3=Marco | journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General | volume=37 | issue=18 | pages=4939–4954 | bibcode=2004JPhA...37.4939R }}</ref> labyrinth,<ref>{{cite journal | arxiv=solv-int/9902009 | doi=10.1142/S0217979294001512 | title=A Critical Ising Model on the Labyrinth | date=1994 | last1=Baake | first1=M. | last2=Grimm | first2=U. | last3=Baxter | first3=R.J. | journal=International Journal of Modern Physics B | volume=08 | issue=25n26 | pages=3579–3600 | bibcode=1994IJMPB...8.3579B }}</ref> lattices with twisted boundaries,<ref>{{cite arXiv | eprint=hep-th/0209048 | last1=Grimm | first1=Uwe | title=Duality and conformal twisted boundaries in the Ising model | date=2002 }}</ref> [[chiral Potts model]],<ref>{{cite journal | arxiv=0905.1924 | doi=10.1088/1742-5468/2009/08/P08012 | title=Duality and symmetry in chiral Potts model | date=2009 | last1=Roan | first1=Shi-Shyr | journal=Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment | issue=8 | article-number=P08012 | bibcode=2009JSMTE..08..012R }}</ref> and many others.

One of the consequences of Kramers–Wannier duality is an exact correspondence in the spectrum of excitations on each side of the critical point.   This was recently demonstrated via [[N. Peter Armitage|THz spectroscopy]] in [[Kitaev chain]]s.<ref>{{cite journal | arxiv=2009.14189 | doi=10.1038/s41567-021-01208-0 | title=Duality and domain wall dynamics in a twisted Kitaev chain | date=2021 | last1=Morris | first1=C. J. | last9=McQueen | first9=T. M. | last10=Koohpayeh | first10=S. M. | last11=Kaul | first11=Ribhu K. | last12=Armitage | first12=N. P. | journal=Nature Physics | volume=17 | issue=7 | pages=832–836 | bibcode=2021NatPh..17..832M }}</ref>

==Derivation==
We define first the variables. In the two-dimensional square lattice Ising model the number of horizontal and vertical links are taken to be equal. The couplings <math> J, J' </math> of the spins  <math>\sigma_i</math> in the two directions are different, and one sets <math>K^*=\beta J</math> and <math>L^* =\beta J'</math> with <math>\beta = 1/kT</math>.
The low temperature expansion of the <math>N</math> spin  partition function <math>Z_N</math> for (K<sup>*</sup>,L<sup>*</sup>) 
obtained from the standard expansion

:::<math> Z_N(K^*,L^*) = 2\sum_{P \subset \Lambda_D} e^{K^*(N-2s)}e^{L^*(N-2r)}</math>
is 
:::<math> Z_N(K^*,L^*) = 2 e^{N(K^*+L^*)} \sum_{ P \subset \Lambda_D} (e^{-2L^*})^r(e^{-2K^*})^s  </math>,
the factor 2 originating from a spin-flip symmetry for each <math>P</math>.
Here the sum over <math>P</math> stands for summation over closed polygons on the lattice resulting in the graphical correspondence from the sum over spins with values <math>\pm 1</math>.

By using the following transformation to variables <math>(K, L)</math>, i.e.

:::<math> \tanh K = e^{-2L^*}, \ \tanh L = e^{-2K^*} </math>

one obtains

:::<math> Z_N(K^*,L^*) = 2(\tanh K \; \tanh L)^{-N/2} \sum_{P} v^r w^s </math>
:::<math> = 2(\sinh 2K \; \sinh 2L)^{-N/2} Z_N(K,L) </math>

where <math>v = \tanh K</math> and <math>w =\tanh L</math> .  This yields a mapping relation between the low temperature expansion <math>Z_N(K^*, L^*)</math> and  the high-temperature expansion <math>Z_N(K,L)</math> described as duality (here Kramers-Wannier duality). With the help of the relations
:::<math>\tanh 2x = \frac{2\tanh x}{1+\tanh^2x}, \; \sinh 2x = 2\sinh x\cosh x </math>

the above hyperbolic tangent relations defining <math>K</math> and <math>L</math> can be written more symmetrically as

:::<math>\, \sinh 2K^* \sinh 2L = 1, \;\; \sinh 2L^* \sinh 2K = 1.</math>

With the free energy per site in the [[thermodynamic limit]]

:::<math> f(K,L) = \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} f_N(K,L) = -kT \lim_{N\rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{N} \log Z_N(K,L) </math>

the Kramers–Wannier duality gives

:::<math> f(K^*,L^*) = f(K,L) + \frac{1}{2} kT \log(\sinh 2K \sinh 2L) </math>

In the isotropic case where ''K = L'', if there is a critical point at ''K = K<sub>c</sub>'' then there is another at ''K = K<sup>*</sup><sub>c</sub>''. Hence, in the case of there being a unique critical point, it would be located at ''K = K<sup>*</sup> = K<sup>*</sup><sub>c</sub>'', implying  ''sinh 2K<sub>c</sub> = 1'', yielding 

:::<math> kT_c = 2.2692J </math>.
The result can also be written and is obtained below as
:::<math> e^{2K_c}= 1+\sqrt{2}. </math>

== Kramers-Wannier duality in other contexts==

The Kramers-Wannier duality appears also  in other contexts.<ref>{{cite journal | arxiv=hep-th/9803201 | doi=10.1088/1126-6708/2002/05/049 | title=(Non-)Abelian Kramers-Wannier Duality and Topological Field Theory | date=2002 | last1=Severa | first1=Pavol | journal=Journal of High Energy Physics | issue=5 | page=049 | bibcode=2002JHEP...05..049S }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | arxiv=hep-th/0206162 | doi=10.1088/1126-6708/2002/05/049 | title=(Non-)Abelian Kramers-Wannier Duality and Topological Field Theory | date=2002 | last1=Severa | first1=Pavol | journal=Journal of High Energy Physics | issue=5 | page=049 | bibcode=2002JHEP...05..049S }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | arxiv=cond-mat/9803388 | doi=10.1016/S0375-9601(97)00225-9 | title=Five-loop for random Ising model and marginal spin dimensionality for cubic systems | date=1997 | last1=Shalaev | first1=B.N. | last2=Antonenko | first2=S.A. | last3=Sokolov | first3=A.I. | journal=Physics Letters A | volume=230 | issue=1–2 | pages=105–110 }}</ref> We consider here particularly the two-dimensional theory of a scalar field <math>\Phi.</math><ref>{{cite arXiv | eprint=cond-mat/0110205 | last1=Shalaev | first1=Boris N. | title=Kramers-Wannier symmetry and strong-weak-coupling duality in the two-dimensional &Phi;<sup>4</sup> field model | date=2001 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | arxiv=cond-mat/9908068 | doi=10.1088/0305-4470/32/42/302 | title=Duality symmetry, strong-coupling expansion and universal critical amplitudes in two-dimensional Phi<sup>4</sup>field models | date=1999 | last1=Jug | first1=Giancarlo | last2=Shalaev | first2=Boris N. | journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General | volume=32 | issue=42 | pages=7249–7261 | bibcode=1999JPhA...32.7249J }}</ref> In this case a more convenient variable than <math>\sinh (2K)</math>is
:::<math> s(K):= \exp(2K)\tanh(K).</math>
With this expression one can construct the [[self-dual quantity]] 
:::<math> \xi^2:=\frac{s(K)}{(1-s(K))^2}=\frac{s(K^*)}{(1-s(K^*))^2}.</math>
In field theory contexts the quantity <math>\xi</math> is called [[correlation length]]. Next set
:::<math> \beta(K):= \xi\frac{dK}{d\xi}=\frac{2s(K)(1-s(K))}{(1+s(K))[ds(K)/dK]}.</math>
This function is the [[beta function]] of [[renormalization]] theory. Now suppose there is a value <math>K^*</math> of <math>K</math> for which <math>\beta(K^*) =0</math>,  i.e. <math>s(K^*)=1</math>. The zero of the beta function is usually related to a symmetry - but only if the zero is unique. The solution of <math>s(K^*)=+1</math> yields (obtained with MAPLE)
:::<math> K^*= i\pi + \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+\sqrt{2}), \;\; \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+\sqrt{2}), \;\; \ln\sqrt{{1-\sqrt2}}</math>.
Only the second solution is real and gives the critical value of Kramers and Wannier as
:::<math> \exp(2K^*) = 1 +\sqrt{2}</math>.
